stories.headline: Commission guidance clarifies battery passport data
stories.consequence: The 71-point overview distinguishes launch requirements from conditional and later disclosures.

stories.headline: General battery labelling did not automatically begin on 18 August
stories.consequence: The implementing act is still pending, while 18 February 2027 remains fixed for the QR code and battery passport.

stories.headline: Operational trials expose supplier-evidence gaps
stories.consequence: Carbon data, governance and third-party verification remain difficult across upstream tiers.

stories.headline: UN/CEFACT opens review of a global passport framework
stories.consequence: P1143 and ISO 25534-1 may influence international trust, governance and interoperability.

transcript: This is the yellow3 Digital Product Passport briefing for Monday, 24 August 2026.

The main development comes from the European Commission. On Friday, it published updated guidance for the Digital Product Passport required for electric-vehicle batteries, e-bike and e-scooter batteries, and industrial batteries above two kilowatt-hours.

The document brings 71 data points into one structured overview. But that number needs context. It does not mean every company must complete 71 fields on day one. Each data point is classified as mandatory, optional, conditional, or not required when the passport rules begin in February 2027.
The update also clarifies that some information comes later. Responsible-sourcing reporting is not required at the February launch, while recycled-content disclosures depend on further EU rules.
The Commission is equally clear that this is guidance. It does not introduce new legal requirements and should not be treated as an authoritative interpretation of the Regulation.
A second point matters because the market is already misreading the calendar.

The general battery-labelling requirements were widely associated with 18 August 2026. But the Regulation says those requirements apply on that date, or 18 months after the relevant implementing act enters into force, whichever is later.
That implementing act is still pending. Therefore, the general labelling requirements did not automatically begin last week.

The QR code and Digital Product Passport deadline is different. For electric-vehicle batteries, e-bike and e-scooter batteries, and industrial batteries above two kilowatt-hours, 18 February 2027 remains the fixed date.
Industry trials are also exposing the real implementation challenge.
The Global Battery Alliance has 17 supply-chain partnerships participating in its operational trials. The cell manufacturers involved account for 80 percent of global production.
Their work is focused on supplier data, carbon-footprint calculations, data governance and third-party verification. In at least one trial, primary carbon data did not yet reach the mining tier.
That is where implementation becomes difficult.
One additional development is on our strategic radar. UN/CEFACT has opened the public review of project P1143, a global Digital Product Passport framework linked to ISO 25534, Part One.

The consultation runs until 12 October. It is not new EU legislation, and the review opened earlier in August, but it may influence how trust, governance and interoperability are handled internationally.
The conclusion this week is simple.
The European requirements are becoming clearer. Global standardisation is moving forward. And the real bottleneck is no longer creating a QR code.
It is obtaining structured, verifiable and updateable evidence across the supply chain.
That is this week’s Digital Product Passport briefing from yellow3 Research Intelligence.

stories.headline: Less than 1% of textile waste becomes new textile
stories.consequence: Scaling textile-to-textile recycling to 15% by 2035 is estimated to require €8-11 billion in capital.

stories.headline: EU textile responsibility schemes are due by April 2028
stories.consequence: Producers will finance collection, sorting, reuse and recycling, with fees linked to ecodesign performance.

stories.headline: Destroying unsold clothing and footwear is now prohibited
stories.consequence: The ban applies to large companies; standardised disclosure of discarded unsold products starts in February 2027.

stories.headline: Registering a passport does not verify its product claims
stories.consequence: A registered passport can prove existence, but the responsible business still owns the accuracy and evidence.

transcript: Good morning.
This week, fashion's Digital Product Passport story stopped being about a QR code.
It became about who pays for a product after it has been sold.
Four developments. One clear conclusion.
First, a new analysis published by Reuters shows the scale of the problem.
Less than one percent of textile waste is currently recycled into new textiles, while global textile waste is expected to increase by more than forty percent by 2035.

According to modelling by ReHubs and Boston Consulting Group, Europe may need between eight and eleven billion euros in capital investment to reach just fifteen percent textile-to-textile recycling by 2035.
The technology is developing. The economic system around it is not ready.
Second, European Union law requires every Member State to establish an Extended Producer Responsibility scheme for textiles and footwear by the 17th of April 2028.
Producers will finance the collection, sorting, reuse and recycling of the products they place on each national market.
Their contributions will be based on product weight and, where appropriate, quantity. The fees will then be adjusted using relevant ecodesign requirements.
In other words, product sustainability data is beginning to have a direct financial value.
Third, the prohibition on destroying unsold clothing and footwear already applies to large companies.
From February 2027, businesses must also use a standard European format to disclose the unsold products they discard.
What happens to a product after production can no longer remain invisible.
Fourth, the European Digital Product Passport Registry is now live and undergoing testing before the first mandatory battery passports arrive in February 2027.
Businesses can register product identifiers through the Registry interface or connect directly through its API.
But registration is not the same as verification.
A registration record can prove that a passport exists. It cannot prove that every environmental, material or recycling claim inside the passport is true.
The business placing the product on the market still owns that responsibility.
And that brings us to this week's conclusion.
The Digital Product Passport is becoming the information layer connecting product design, compliance, waste fees, sorting and recycling.
Businesses that treat it as a webpage or QR code added at the end will have started in the wrong place.
The real work begins with the product data, where it comes from, what evidence supports it, who is responsible for it, and how it stays accurate.
The question is no longer:
"Who can generate our passport?"
The question is:
"Can we prove our product well enough for the systems now forming around it?"
That is this week's Digital Product Passport briefing from yellow3 Research Intelligence.

stories.headline: Factory data can generate the passport
stories.consequence: An open-source OPC reference solution derives product-specific passport data from production.

stories.headline: Global Digital Product Passport standardisation begins in Berlin
stories.consequence: ISO/IEC JTC 5 meets 7-9 September with 32 participating and 16 observing members.

transcript: Good morning, and welcome to the yellow3 Monday Morning Briefing for 7 September 2026.
The main Digital Product Passport story this week is not another deadline.
It is the infrastructure now starting to form around it.
First, to Brussels.
The European Commission’s current roadmap points to September for the decision covering the final two horizontal Digital Product Passport standards.
Six standards have already been cited.
The remaining areas include access rights, information security, confidentiality, and the authentication and reliability of passport data.
That is important because the technical framework is getting much closer to completion.
But there is one distinction worth making.
September is a standards milestone.
It is not a new compliance deadline for another product category.
Now to implementation.
On 3 September, the OPC Foundation presented an open-source reference implementation showing how a Digital Product Passport can be generated directly from industrial production data.
In the example, a product is tracked through manufacturing by serial number.
Data from the production process can then be used to calculate product-specific information, including carbon footprint, collect relevant quality information, and generate the passport itself.
That is a significant development.
Because it points to a very different future from the one many companies are still preparing for.
The Digital Product Passport may not become another system where somebody manually enters information after a product is made.
Instead, it can increasingly become an output of the production process itself.
The OPC Foundation is clear that this is still a reference implementation, not a finished compliance product.
But the direction matters.
And there is another important development today.
From 7 to 9 September, the new ISO and IEC Joint Technical Committee for the Digital Product Passport is holding its first meeting in Berlin.
Thirty-two countries are participating, with another sixteen observing.
The objective is international interoperability.
And that takes the Digital Product Passport discussion beyond Europe.

Last week, the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific also brought Digital Product Passports into a wider discussion on cross-border trade, alongside international standards organisations, digital trade infrastructure and global logistics.
Taken together, the signal is becoming clearer.
The Digital Product Passport is starting to move beyond being treated simply as a European sustainability compliance requirement.
It is becoming part of a much larger technical infrastructure connecting products, factories, supply chains, regulators and international trade.
And for businesses, that changes the question.
It is becoming less about:
Which Digital Product Passport platform should we buy?
And much more about:
Can we produce trusted product information at the source, maintain the evidence behind it, and move that information reliably across systems?
That is where the real implementation challenge is starting to appear.
We will keep watching the evidence.
This is yellow3.
